mastery.oneLine: A seven-step osteopathic sequence of gentle, rhythmic shoulder movements used for stiff shoulders.
mastery.whatItIs: The Spencer technique is a fixed sequence of seven shoulder movements, performed with the patient lying on their side. It is used for stiffness such as adhesive capsulitis. Each step gently moves the shoulder toward its limit in a rhythmic way.
mastery.analogy: Like a warm-up routine: seven short moves that gradually loosen the shoulder in a planned order.
coreIdeas: The sequence covers extension, flexion, circumduction (with compression and traction), abduction, adduction with internal rotation, and a final traction step.
Rhythm and gentle pressure matter more than force.
Assess shoulder movement before and after.

terms.meaning: Frozen shoulder: painful, progressive stiffness of the shoulder joint capsule.
Moving the arm in a circle.

whenToUse: A stiff shoulder in the stiff or recovery phase, once other causes have been screened.
whenNot: Shoulder fracture, dislocation, severe pain or infection.
Neurological signs, or pain that rises sharply during the steps.

steps.title: Screen and assess range
steps.detail: Record how far the arm lifts and rotates.

steps.title: Position the patient
steps.detail: Lie on the unaffected side with the shoulder supported.

steps.title: Steps 1-2
steps.detail: Gently take the shoulder into extension and flexion within comfort.

steps.title: Steps 3-4
steps.detail: Perform circumduction first with gentle compression, then with gentle traction.

steps.title: Steps 5-6
steps.detail: Move the arm into abduction, then adduction with internal rotation.

steps.title: Step 7 and retest
steps.detail: Finish with gentle rhythmic traction and then retest range.

mastery.dose: Typical teaching range: each step performed gently for several rhythmic repetitions. Follow your training and keep within comfort.

example.patient: Margaret, 63, stiff right shoulder for four months, can lift to 90 degrees.
example.assessment: Painful and stiff, with no fracture and no nerve signs.
example.treatment: Seven-step sequence performed gently in side-lying.
example.reassess: She can lift to 105 degrees and pain is slightly reduced. A home exercise plan follows.

mistakes: Treating the sequence as a cure.

selfTest.q: What is it commonly used for?
selfTest.a: Stiff shoulders such as adhesive capsulitis.

mastery.recap: Seven gentle steps, then retest and exercise.
mastery.evidence: Evidence is limited to small studies. It may help stiffness for some, but it is not proven better than other approaches.

depth.why: The Spencer sequence is a fixed order of passive and assisted shoulder movements, commonly taught as seven, used in the osteopathic tradition to improve mobility and ease symptoms. The movements put the glenohumeral joint and its surrounding tissues through rhythmic, graded range in several planes. The likely effect is short-term mobility and symptom relief from graded movement and attention, as with other articulatory methods, rather than a correction of a specific lesion.
choose: Use it when a stiff, painful shoulder needs gentle, graded passive movement and the examination excludes instability or a tear that needs protection.
Prefer targeted treatment when the examination points to a specific structure.
Adapt the order and range to the patient's tolerance; the sequence is a framework, not a fixed prescription.
parameters: A fixed order of gentle movements through the shoulder's range, adapted to the patient's tolerance
Side-lying with the trunk and scapula stabilised, the arm supported
A few smooth repetitions of each movement, within comfort and short of provoking pain
Active range and pain on the provoking movement after the sequence
depth.progress: Progress from assisted to active movement through the new range, then to loaded and overhead function. Reduce the passive sequence as soon as the patient can move the arm actively through most of the range.
measure: Active and passive range of elevation and rotation, measured the same way before and after
Pain on the painful arc or reach, on the same scale
Function: a task the patient finds hard, such as reaching overhead or behind the back
depth.evidence: The Spencer sequence is a documented osteopathic approach, but high-quality trials that isolate this exact sequence are sparse. General evidence for shoulder mobility work cannot be treated as technique-specific proof.
pitfalls: Moving a shoulder with an unrecognised cuff tear or instability through forceful end range.
Applying the sequence rigidly regardless of irritability.
Stopping at passive movement without handing the range back to the patient actively.
screen: Recent dislocation or fracture, acute cuff tear or marked instability
Unexplained severe weakness or neurological signs

heading.en: The seven Spencer movements, in order
heading.ur: Spencer ki saat movements, tarteeb se

intro.en: Patient side-lying with the stiff shoulder up. One hand steadies the shoulder girdle; the other guides the arm through each movement to a comfortable end, with a small rhythmic stretch there. Work gently, in the same order every time, and retest after the seventh.
intro.ur: Patient side-lying, akra hua shoulder upar. Ek haath shoulder girdle ko steady rakhta hai; doosra haath arm ko har movement mein comfortable end tak le jata hai aur wahan chhoti rhythmic stretch deta hai. Narmi se, har dafa wahi tarteeb, aur saatvi ke baad retest karein.

what.en: Takes the shoulder back into extension.
what.ur: Shoulder ko peeche extension mein le jata hai.

en: Let the arm hang forward a little.
Move it back to the comfortable end.
Add 2 or 3 small rhythmic stretches there.
ur: Arm ko thora agay latakne dein.
Isay comfortable end tak peeche le jayein.
Wahan 2 ya 3 chhoti rhythmic stretches dein.

tag.en: Elbow bent, arm forward and up
tag.ur: Elbow bent, arm agay aur upar

what.en: Lifts the arm forward and up with the elbow bent.
what.ur: Elbow bent rakh kar arm ko agay aur upar uthata hai.

en: Bend the elbow and support it.
Raise the arm forward toward the head.
Give small rhythmic stretches at the end.
ur: Elbow bend karein aur support dein.
Arm ko agay sir ki taraf uthayein.
End par chhoti rhythmic stretches dein.

what.en: Makes slow circles while gently pressing the joint together.
what.ur: Joint ko narmi se dabate hue slow circles banata hai.

en: Hold the bent elbow.
Press the arm gently into the socket.
Draw slow circles both ways.
ur: Bent elbow pakdein.
Arm ko narmi se socket ki taraf dabayein.
Dono taraf slow circles banayein.

tag.ur: Chhote circles, joint halka khincha hua

what.en: The same circles, now with a gentle pull away from the socket.
what.ur: Wahi circles, ab socket se door halke khinchao ke saath.

en: Hold the arm and pull gently along its length.
Keep the pull light and steady.
Draw slow circles both ways.
ur: Arm pakdein aur lambai ke rukh halka kheinchein.
Khinchao halka aur steady rakhein.
Dono taraf slow circles banayein.

tag.en: Arm out to the side and up

what.en: Lifts the arm out to the side with the elbow bent.
what.ur: Elbow bent rakh kar arm ko side se uthata hai.

en: Support the bent elbow.
Raise the arm out to the side to the comfortable end.
Add small rhythmic stretches.
ur: Bent elbow ko support dein.
Arm ko side se comfortable end tak uthayein.
Chhoti rhythmic stretches dein.

what.en: Brings the arm across and the hand toward the small of the back.
what.ur: Arm ko across aur haath ko kamar ki taraf le jata hai.

en: Place the patient's hand toward the lower back.
Move gently to the comfortable end.
Give small rhythmic stretches, never forcing.
ur: Patient ka haath kamar ki taraf rakhein.
Narmi se comfortable end tak le jayein.
Chhoti rhythmic stretches dein, zabardasti kabhi nahi.

what.en: Finishes with a gentle rhythmic pull along the arm, then retest.
what.ur: Aakhir mein arm ke rukh halka rhythmic khinchao, phir retest.

en: Hold the forearm with the arm straight.
Apply a gentle, rhythmic pull.
Retest reach, pain and function, then give exercises.
ur: Arm seedha rakh kar forearm pakdein.
Halka rhythmic khinchao dein.
Reach, pain aur function retest karein, phir exercises dein.

watch.en: Stop for sharp pain, numbness or a recent fracture or dislocation.
watch.ur: Tez dard, sunn-pan ya recent fracture/dislocation par ruk jayein.

urdu.short: Spencer technique shoulder ke liye saat gentle, rhythmic movements ka osteopathic sequence hai. Stiff shoulder mein selected cases ke liye use ho sakta hai, magar force nahi karni aur fracture, dislocation ya doosri serious causes pehle screen karni hain.

details.heading: Yeh kya hai?
details.text: Patient side-lying position mein hota hai aur shoulder ko saat movements ke fixed sequence se gently move kiya jata hai. Adhesive capsulitis jaisi stiffness mein istemal kiya jata raha hai; har step shoulder ko rhythm ke sath comfortable limit ki taraf le jata hai.

details.heading: Misal se samjhein
details.text: Warm-up routine ki tarah saat chhoti movements shoulder ko planned order mein dheere dheere move karti hain. Yeh analogy hai, cure ka claim nahi.

details.heading: Bunyadi ideas aur terms
details.text: Sequence mein extension, flexion, circumduction compression aur traction ke sath, abduction, adduction with internal rotation aur aakhir mein traction shamil hoti hai. Rhythm aur gentle pressure force se zyada aham hain. Adhesive capsulitis frozen shoulder hai; circumduction arm ko circle mein move karna; side-lying unaffected side par letna; articulation repeated gentle joint movement hai.

details.heading: Kab use karein / kab nahi
details.text: Screening ke baad stiff ya recovery phase ke shoulder mein, aur trained practitioners ke liye. Shoulder fracture, dislocation, severe pain, infection, neurological signs, ya steps ke dauran dard tez barhne par use na karein.

details.heading: Steps
details.text:
1. Range record karein.
2. Patient ko unaffected side par shoulder support ke sath litaayein.
3. Extension aur flexion gently karein.
4. Circumduction pehle gentle compression aur phir traction ke sath karein.
5. Abduction, phir adduction with internal rotation karein.
6. Gentle rhythmic traction se finish karke range dobara check karein.

details.heading: Dose
details.text: Har step ki chand gentle rhythmic repetitions; apni training follow karein aur patient ke comfort ke andar rahein.

details.heading: Clinical example — source ka scenario
details.text: Source mein Margaret, 63 saal ki, chaar mahine se stiff right shoulder rakhti hain aur 90 degrees tak lift kar pati hain. Fracture aur nerve signs nahi. Side-lying mein gentle seven-step sequence ke baad lift 105 degrees tak aur pain thora behtar hota hai; home exercise plan follow hota hai. Yeh teaching scenario hai.

details.heading: Aam ghaltiyan aur self-test
details.text: Pain ke aage force karna, screening skip karna, ya sequence ko cure samajhna. Kitne steps? Saat. Aam use? Adhesive capsulitis jaisa stiff shoulder.

details.heading: Recap aur evidence
details.text: Saat gentle steps, phir retest aur exercise. Evidence chhoti studies tak limited hai; kuch logon ki stiffness mein madad ho sakti hai, magar doosri approaches se behtar hona prove nahi.

deeper.heading: Clinical reasoning
deeper.text: Spencer shoulder sequence osteopathic manual approach hai jo shoulder region ki mobility ko a series of movements ke zariye assess ya treat kar sakta hai. Pehle shoulder history, trauma, irritability, active range aur neurological/vascular signs assess karein.

deeper.heading: Sequence aur adaptation
deeper.text: Sequence ke movements patient ki tolerance aur clinical findings ke mutabiq adapt kiye jate hain. Exact sequence aur hand placements supervised training se seekhein; painful range mein mechanically complete karna zaroori nahi.

deeper.heading: Common mistakes aur precautions
deeper.text: Acute fracture/dislocation suspicion, post-operative restrictions ya severe pain ko ignore karke sequence perform na karein. Symptoms barhne, guarding ya unusual response par stop karein aur relevant medical assessment consider karein.

deeper.heading: Reassessment aur evidence
deeper.text: Shoulder range, pain aur daily tasks ko sequence se pehle aur baad compare karein. Aik manual sequence har shoulder diagnosis ka solution nahi; exercise, load management aur condition-specific care ko saath rakhein.

cue.wake: Seven shoulder moves? The arm just registered for an entire semester.
cue.question: Must every patient complete all seven stages, even if one hurts?
cue.answer: No. Safety, examination and functional goals determine which parts are suitable.
cue.easy: Articulatory movement = a joint moved gently through a controlled path.
cue.remember: Seven stages to learn; one real-life goal to test.

worldDeep.opening: A tailor's assistant can lift fabric all day but struggles to reach behind the back for a jacket. When told that the Spencer method has seven movements, the patient asks, 'Seven? Is my shoulder enrolling in a full semester?' The number is memorable, but it is not magic. The classical Spencer sequence is an osteopathic articulatory shoulder approach; the stages guide structured exploration of shoulder motion, not seven guaranteed fixes.

principles.title: Seven movements are a teaching sequence, not a dose guarantee
principles.body: Traditional descriptions commonly include extension, flexion, circumduction with compression, circumduction with traction, abduction, internal rotation, and a final joint-pumping component. Exact sequence order and named modifications vary by school. A chapter should explain the purpose of each stage, not imply every patient must tolerate all seven.

principles.title: Shoulder movement involves more than one joint
principles.body: Glenohumeral motion interacts with scapular upward rotation, posterior tilt, thoracic movement and muscle control. A painful reach might involve guarding, weakness or capsular restriction. Treating an apparent stiffness without assessing these contributors misses the real task.

principles.title: Articulatory input must stay controlled
principles.body: The approach uses gently guided movement, often near comfortable ranges, with clear support and stabilization. It is not a license to force an end-range circumduction in a shoulder with instability, recent dislocation or suspected tear.

principles.title: Stage names describe directions, not a self-taught recipe
principles.body: Without hands-on training, a list of seven movements does not adequately specify stabilizing hand contact, scapular control, traction magnitude, patient position or stop criteria. A responsible education chapter explains the movements while protecting the reader from false confidence.

principles.title: Movement and function determine value
principles.body: The goal is not to complete a ceremonial sequence. A patient may benefit from carefully selected tolerable movement and active exercises without ever needing every historical step.

assessment.title: Differentiate painful arc, capsular loss and weakness
assessment.body: Check onset, injury mechanism, passive versus active elevation, external rotation, apprehension, cervical referral and meaningful tasks such as dressing. A shoulder that is weak after injury is not simply 'tight'.

assessment.title: Protect vulnerable anatomy
assessment.body: Screen suspected fracture, instability, acute cuff tear, neurovascular signs, post-surgical restrictions, inflammatory pathology and severe resting pain. With a recent dislocation, forced circumduction can be hazardous.

assessment.title: Measure a comparable sign
assessment.body: Choose controlled shoulder flexion, external rotation, reaching behind the back or placing a hand on a shelf. Note scapular compensation and symptom behavior.

assessment.title: Decide whether passive movement fits
assessment.body: If the presentation supports comfortable mobilization as an adjunct, consent and training are prerequisites. Some cases warrant mainly active control or medical referral, not an articulatory sequence.

application.title: Stage 1 — Extension: explore reaching behind
application.body: In classical teaching, supported glenohumeral extension explores comfortable posterior reach. Observe scapular compensation and avoid forcing anterior shoulder pain or instability. Ask what the patient experiences, not whether the movement looks impressive.

application.title: Stage 2 — Flexion: explore a forward reach
application.body: Gentle assisted flexion can reveal movement tolerance during the route toward an overhead task. Protect the scapula and avoid pushing through sharp pain. Active participation is integrated where appropriate.

application.title: Stage 3 — Circumduction with compression
application.body: A small controlled circular movement with an appropriately directed gentle approximation is described in traditional teaching. This is not heavy joint loading; exact force and contact require qualified practical instruction, especially with an irritable shoulder.

application.title: Stage 4 — Circumduction with traction
application.body: Classical variations contrast the previous input with gentle distraction during controlled movement. Screen instability and apprehension before any distraction; a vulnerable joint should not be 'stretched into place'.

application.title: Stage 5 — Abduction
application.body: Supported movement away from the side explores the frontal-plane pathway and scapulohumeral coordination. Watch for painful arc, trunk lean and compensatory shoulder hiking. A smaller comfortable excursion may be more useful than an impressive end range.

application.title: Stage 6 — Internal rotation
application.body: A supported, appropriate rotation movement helps explore tasks such as reaching to dress. Never force a hand behind the back or torque a shoulder that guards or shows instability.

application.title: Stage 7 — Joint pumping
application.body: Traditional Spencer descriptions include a final gentle rhythmic joint-pump element. Its historical proposed circulatory benefits should not be treated as proven. It is optional and inappropriate if screening or symptom response advises against it.

application.title: The real final stage — independent reassessment
application.body: After removing the therapist's hands, test the same dressing, reach or rotation goal and agree on graded active shoulder exercise. This clinically meaningful eighth 'scene' matters more than mechanically checking all seven stages.

caseStudy.scene: The tailor's assistant points to a jacket: 'My arm gets stuck right when I try to get into the sleeve.' The therapist notes restricted and uncomfortable motion, but the patient's ability to control the movement is equally important.
caseStudy.findings: Passive range is limited but not all directions behave alike. Screening suggests a suitable conservative rehabilitation presentation; active motion, strength and symptoms are documented before a manual trial.
caseStudy.decision: The clinician explains the Spencer framework, chooses selected comfortable stages rather than forcing the entire classical sequence, and watches pain and scapular response. The patient practises active reach afterwards.
caseStudy.twist: A selected gentle stage feels easier, yet the jacket task barely changes. The therapist resists the temptation to complete the remaining steps simply because there are seven boxes on a list.
caseStudy.finish: The plan shifts toward graded functional shoulder movement and relevant strengthening. The Spencer approach remains a way to structure clinical exploration, not the diagnosis or guaranteed solution.

worldDeep.dose: There is no universally established seven-stage dose or mandatory number of repetitions. Choose the components, movement amplitude and session exposure according to irritability, joint stability and supervised training. Never complete every stage at the expense of comfort or patient consent.
worldDeep.caution: Avoid forcible articulatory motion with suspected rotator-cuff rupture, recent dislocation, fracture, substantial instability, active inflammatory flare or prohibited postoperative ranges. Reassess for new numbness, vascular signs or major weakness.

evidence.known: The historical sequence is described in osteopathic teaching. Supported range-of-motion and graded exercise can form part of selected shoulder rehabilitation programs.
evidence.unknown: Evidence isolating the complete Spencer sequence as superior to contemporary multimodal physiotherapy is limited. Benefits observed from mobilization and exercise generally cannot be assigned specifically to all seven Spencer stages.
evidence.communication: 'This method describes seven traditional shoulder movements. We will use only what your examination and comfort allow, and we will judge the effect by your ability to use the shoulder—not by completing a ritual.'

worldDeep.memoryHook: Seven movements make a chapter. The jacket gets to write the ending.

checks.question: Why should a clinician not automatically complete all seven stages?
checks.answer: Different shoulder conditions, irritability, instability and patient goals require selective movement. Completing the list is not an evidence-based outcome.

checks.question: What does a joint-pump stage prove if the patient's pain improves?
checks.answer: A response may be useful, but it does not validate proposed fluid-pumping mechanisms or prove superiority of the whole named sequence.
